<reason>A wins through clearer causal reasoning and more responsive rebuttal. B establishes genuine discovery and classification costs, which A acknowledges, but repeatedly treats avoiding harmful recommendations as worthless unless the algorithm itself is repaired. A also exposes the unsupported leap from a more partisan recommendation audience to greater societal polarization or civic silence. B's unspecified ranking reform does not uniquely favor keeping recommendations on by default. A's classification safeguards and net-benefit weighing remain underdeveloped, limiting the margin.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A decisively answers B's “the disease remains” objection: reducing involuntary exposure can reduce harm even when opted-in users retain the same risk. B repeats its objection rather than explaining why that avoided exposure has no value or is outweighed by lost discovery.</best_rebuttal>
